Something interesting is happening around fast matrix multiplication.

@WeinsteinOmri has been exploring a question at the centre of the FMM debate: why do algorithms with better theoretical complexity often struggle to outperform conventional matrix multiplication on actual hardware?

His work with Kevin Pratt and Yahel Uffenheimer explores FFT-based convolutions as an alternative to traditional Strassen-style recursion.
https://t.co/VdHDkTx6Cn

Now @PassRafael has presented a constructive proof showing that the matrix multiplication exponent satisfies ω ≤ 9/4, using polynomial packings to explicitly construct the underlying algebraic identity.
https://t.co/EPjARHQMEa

These are different approaches, but they point towards the same broader problem: making matrix multiplication cheaper.

And there are some important questions worth asking:

If we can push the exponent down to 2.25, what still prevents that improvement from translating into practical GPU performance?

Could FFT-based approaches offer a more practical direction than recursive algorithms, or will memory movement and communication remain the bigger bottlenecks?

At what matrix size does asymptotic superiority become an actual engineering advantage?

And what happens when matrix multiplication is not just an AI workload, but also the computational foundation of a proof-of-useful-work protocol?

This is where @prlnet makes the discussion particularly interesting.

pearl-2:native  is building around useful computation, with matrix multiplication serving as a workload for its cuPOW approach. 
Its ability to adapt to improvements in the algorithms used to perform that computation is an important part of the bigger picture.

A faster algorithm changes the cost of doing the work. That has implications for the economics of useful compute, verification and the assumptions behind the protocol.

Could proof-of-useful-work ecosystems like Pearl become one of the places where advances in computational mathematics translate into real economic value?

That's a much bigger conversation than simply finding a faster way to multiply matrices.

Here are the 5 narratives I'm watching before the markets pump:

1. AI Inference

Every time someone uses Claude or an AI agent, somebody pays for the computing power behind it. That's inference.

As agents do more work on their own, that bill keeps getting bigger.

Some crypto projects already let people buy or access that compute through their tokens.

I'd check two things. Are there real paying customers? And does that demand actually flow back to the token?

• $VVV $ORBIO

2. Proof of Useful Work / AI Compute

Bitcoin miners burn a huge amount of computing power just to secure the network.

Pearl and Nockchain are betting the same kind of hardware can do useful work (AI models, ZK proofs) and still earn rewards.

Bittensor goes broader and pays people for useful AI contributions.

The catch is that a network can have thousands of GPUs running with nobody actually paying to use them.

So the number I care about is revenue from real customers vs rewards paid by printing new tokens.

• $PEARL $NOCK $TAO

3. Privacy

Right now anyone can look up a wallet and see the savings in it and every payment it's ever made.

Businesses and AI agents aren't gonna move serious money on rails like that.

Zcash and Monero already do private payments. Newer projects are building private apps and smart contracts.

The obvious risk is regulators. Honestly, I don't have a clean answer to that one.

So I'd trust usage over headlines. That means growth in private transactions and apps that really need privacy to work.

• $ZEC $XMR $NIGHT

4. Quantum Resistance

Quantum computers may one day break the cryptography that protects most crypto wallets. And you can't upgrade a whole blockchain overnight.

The interesting part is that networks are already taking different routes.

NEAR added quantum-safe signatures (ML-DSA) to mainnet in July.

Starknet is aiming to be fully quantum resistant by 2027.

Quantus launched in September with quantum-resistant signatures from day one.

I'm honestly not sure on timing here. So I'd only care which upgrades are actually live, and whether any of it creates demand for the token.

• $QTC $NEAR $STRK

5. Revenue & Buybacks

The part most people still skip is doing the math after dilution.

Say a project buys back $10M while unlocking $50M in new tokens. It's still putting more on the market than it's taking off.

So I'd look at how much revenue actually reaches the token after unlocks and emissions.

• $HYPE $UNI $PUMP

I'd build a watchlist with 2 or 3 projects per sector and check those numbers once a month.

The setup I want is the number getting better while the price hasn't caught up yet.

That gap is usually widest when everyone's scared... like right now.

great report on $PEARL from @minnus & @0xMetaLight.

they're net bullish, but the report backs up a lot of my bear case. some key points:

1) the "useful work" isn't happening yet. fewer than 1% of blocks match a real AI model, and gaming cards run ~82% of hashrate.

2) AI servers have no reason to mine (at today's price). an AI server gives up $1.33-$3.15 of paid AI work for each coin it mines, while a gaming card pays $0.14-$0.23 in power.

3) the only real-world example didn't last. together AI's pearl-powered endpoint launched in may at a 25%+ discount, and was deprecated a couple months later.

4) the useful mining fix has no timeline. the FP8 upgrade would make mining on an AI server about as cheap as mining on a gaming card, but there's no published date, and the draft only works on nvidia's newest chips. so older gaming cards and every AMD card could get shut out, and gaming cards run most of the network today.

5) miners sell fast. about half of pool payouts go straight to one custodian's deposit addresses, and only ~10% is still sitting in miners' wallets a week later.

6) miners who already own their gaming GPUs only pay for power, so they'd stay profitable even if $PEARL fell ~80%. which means their costs give the price little support.

7) the network is concentrated. ~90% of blocks go through pools, kryptex alone mines ~50%, and the top 1% of addresses hold ~71% of supply.

8) transparency is still missing. ~125M $PEARL was issued in launch week, 98% of it has never moved, and the lab still hasn't disclosed its holdings.

the bull case depends on FP8 shipping and AI providers actually mining. until then, holders will have to absorb ~84% supply growth, about $540M of new $PEARL, over the next year.

If you believe what Omri and team have written, Pearl's software stack may make normal workloads more efficient than baseline is today even without mining. Call that -X% for the sake of argument. So rolling out the stack (with mining turned off) should be a net cost advantage for ML providers.

Then, Pearl fp8 mining adds some inference overhead call that +Y%. Inference gets a little bit slower because of mining, but the parameters are tunable. If your workload needs low latency, you mine less and do more inference. If your workload is batch jobs that are OK with latency, you mine more and do inference slower. ML providers turn mining on/off when its profitable.

An added benefit of the (planned) Pearl stack is access to distributed compute jobs. For ML jobs that can be trusted to distribute using privacy attestations and TEE, jobs can eventually be paid for with PRL token. It's a natural network effect to pay for distributed compute with a distributed currency.

So the net takeaways:
- Inference providers likely get a net cost savings from integrating the Pearl stack.
- Depending on workload latency requirements and Pearl price, miners join the network when mining revenue > incremental costs.
- Pearl token is used to pay for distributed compute jobs. It's natural to use a decentralized hard money to pay for decentralized work.

Return on capital brings in miners. Distributed compute brings in token usage. More miners and more token usage increase energy and monetary effects, bringing in pure-SOV buyers.

Over time, Pearl token is likely to be seen as a future on inference compute. Since compute will be payable in Pearl, corporations and individuals have a reason to stockpile the token today to pay for compute tomorrow.

Dependencies: fp8 lands well, continued AI usage, electricity and hardware continue to cost money, team executes well.

$PEARL was hyped as AI Bitcoin: fair launch, no premine, no VCs.

Turns out the lab behind it quietly raised ~$130M.

Per @TheMarker (25th of Oct) $55M equity across two rounds from Lightspeed, Ribbit and Square Peg, plus a separate $75M fund for the company's own GPU array. Israeli outlet ICE matched it to corporate filings. No comment from @prlnet or the founders yet.

I closed my long on the way down. Rode it from 5 figs unrealized back to almost flat, plus a juicy funding bill lol.

The tech is still one of the most interesting things in crypto x AI. But with emissions this high and a launch this concentrated, a big part of the narrative is kinda dead rn imo.

What still holds?

The coin is fair in code. No premine, no token allocation for founders or investors. You either mined PRL or bought it.

What doesn't?

- The start: Difficulty began at the minimum and could only climb ~0.03% per block, so for days blocks came every ~12s vs a 194s target. Day one minted 12.3% of all PRL to date. The first six days minted a third (120M PRL, ~$210M today) on ~1/60th of today's hashrate.

- Emissions: ~1.15M new PRL a day, ~$2M at $1.75, ~23% of daily volume. Hashrate tripled since late Aug, so blocks land every ~161s vs the 194s target. That's +83% to +97% more supply over the next 12 months.

- Mining: One pool found 52.6% of the last 500 blocks, the top five 91.8%.

So why does the raise matter if the coin was fair?

Bc nobody outside the lab knows who owns that supply:

- Do investors or the team hold PRL, and how much of week one did they mine?

- Does the $75M GPU array mine PRL? Pearl GPUs mine as a by-product of inference, and the lab sells inference on its own API.

- Will any of it be locked?

Venice ($VVV) runs the same equity plus token split. But Venice announced its $65M raise, filed a Form D, locked investor tokens and burns part of its revenue. Pearl has none of that and trades at a $3.7B FDV.

Price barely reacted: ~$1.80 when the story broke, $1.75 now, ~29% off the $2.46 ATH.

The real test is Coinbase (roadmap since the 19th of Oct, no date yet). It's the first venue where early miners can sell size into real books, on top of ~1.15M new PRL every day.

What gets me back in?

- Disclosed investor and team holdings, incl. week-one mining
- A clear answer on who controls the GPU fund and whether it mines
- Locks on lab and investor PRL
- Inference revenue that actually reaches the token

A rebound is easy while liquidity is this thin, and if the team fixes this it can run again. I'm just not back in before they answer.

I've enjoyed Jake's coverage on Pearl. Even though I am bullish I think his criticisms are fair, I also think we have more common ground than it appears. Specifically:

-Pearl's emission schedule is the number 1 bear case. A key aspect of a SOV asset is that price goes up, which is harder if you have indiscriminate sellers.

-Concerns around transparency are also valid. Without a "fundamental" business / revenue line, narrative is the main driver of price. An absence of clear communication leads to uncertainty and doubt, which is detrimental to an asset that derives its value from social consensus.

However, on the actual nature of the raise I disagree that it's bearish or leads to a conflict of interest:

To me, token-equity concerns arise for revenue generating protocols, where value accrual is unclear as it is either diluted or completely given to equity holders that act as a senior tranche, with token holders suffering.

Pearl Labs' equity raise causes no conflict of interest since the distinction is clear: Pearl is a SOV asset, while Pearl Labs is an AI infrastructure company that develops Pearl's proof-of-useful-work technology and commercializes inference services. Pearl Labs' success is accretive to the Pearl ecosystem but never extractive, since Pearl is not intended to accrue revenue. If anything the equity raise means 1) Pearl Labs is not reliant on selling PRL to fund operations, 2) it signifies there are powerful forces behind the success of PRL and 3) the raise will add hashrate to the PRL network.

Very strongly disagree that Pearl Labs should introduce PRL buybacks. It would be the quickest way to add a token/equity conflict, as it immediately creates the question of how much value accrues to Pearl Labs vs the token. It also instantly reframes Pearl from an asset trading at 1/30th of ZEC's valuation to an overvalued 1000x P/S token. This is the counterintuitive thing about SOV assets: Flows >>> buybacks, even for huge revenue generating projects like HYPE (although buybacks matter a lot for narrative). Removing a business and letting an asset trade purely as an expression of an idea (e.g. AI BTC) removes company specific and execution risk, stops anchoring the token to a business that needs to grow in line with the price, and also removes its ceiling.

The second controversial point is around centralization and the team mining 5% for themselves. Controversially, I think centralization matters less than people think, even for SOVs. Take MicroStrategy / Bitmine as examples. What matters is centralization among team/VCs who are going to sell. If the team mining a significant amount of tokens means those tokens are effectively out of circulation, I view this as bullish rather than bearish. Of course, this only holds true as long as they don't sell.

Lastly I think it's important to contextualize that a lot of my bullishness comes from a regret minimization framework. Pearl is a nascent SOV, and the concerns around emissions / transparency are very valid. However, it is also one of the most exciting narratives. Just like there is a future where Pearl is insta dumped by institutions that mine it at a low cost basis, there is a future where powerful BTC miners and connected entities rally behind PRL as a new way to monetize their compute through inference, while hashrate increases and fears continue to grow around BTC's security budget.

Thats why, while I see the same risks as Jake, I think that potential of exponential upside does justify a small position, even if just as a hedge to existing BTC/ZEC holdings.

GPU non-determinism forced us to reverse-engineer arithmetic that modern AI hardware does not expose.

The same matrix multiplication can produce different results across @NVIDIA Ampere, Hopper and Lovelace GPUs. The reason is not randomness - it is architecture-specific behavior in the order of accumulation, internal precision, rounding, normalization and handling of subnormal values. That makes exact verification difficult: a CPU re-execution may disagree with a perfectly correct GPU execution.

Hawkeye solves this by systematically probing Tensor Cores with carefully constructed matrix multiplications. These tests recover the hidden numerical pipeline behind each architecture, including how products are grouped, when significands are truncated and when intermediate values are normalized. The recovered behavior is then encoded into a CPU simulator that reproduces the original GPU computation bit-for-bit.

The results show meaningful architectural differences. Ampere uses a two-stage accumulation structure with a 24-bit internal significand, while Hopper combines all 16 products in one stage using 25 bits. Both use truncation-based, round-towards-zero behavior rather than conventional round-to-nearest arithmetic.

Across 100,000 randomly generated matrix multiplications in FP16, BF16 and FP8, Hawkeye reproduced the GPU result with 100% bit-exact accuracy. This creates a foundation for auditors to verify AI training and inference without modifying or slowing down the original GPU workload.

Looking forward, matrix multiplication is only the first step. Extending this approach to attention, fused kernels, distributed training and cryptographic proof systems could make end-to-end, hardware-accurate verification of AI workloads possible.
